newsitem.title: TURKEY: TURK BANKS' LONG-TERM BOND PORTFOLIOS SEEN RISKY.
newsitem.headline: TURK BANKS' LONG-TERM BOND PORTFOLIOS SEEN RISKY.

text.p: The growing amount of long-term government bonds held by Turkish banks creates risks for them because their customers prefer to make shorter-term investments in the bond market, bankers said.

"Private investors do not prefer long-term investments in the bond market, but banks carry large amounts of papers with maturities of more than one year. This widens the maturity gap in the system and raises a maturity risk for banks," Kemal Gurer, assistant general manager at Esbank told Reuters.

Most bond market investors place their money in repo deals of up to one month and some in treasury bills of three-six month maturity, while banks have been buying 13-month bonds issued by the Treasury since December 1996.

"When interest rates are in a downward trend, banks make very good profits by making repo deals with the papers in their portfolios, but if this trend reverses, they will be in a difficult position trying to liquidate their securities," Gurer said.
Banks were forced to buy longer term bonds due to the Treasury's attempt to extend its domestic borrowing maturities to more than one year in late 1996 from six to nine months.

The introduction of foreign currency-denominated bonds and witholding tax on interest income from state securities, followed by an increase in the witholding tax rate fuelled demand for the Treasury's recent long-term issues.

"Investors are not looking for one-year papers. But we have to buy long-term papers and sell them for maturities not longer than six months. There is a maturity gap, so we need new instruments to meet customers' shorter term needs," said a private bank treasury manager.
The maturity gap between banks' deposits and bond portfolios also raises imbalances in the banks' balance sheets.

"Banks' bond portfolio maturities increased to one year, but the average deposit maturity remains below one year. That creates an imbalance between banks' assets and liabilities. It is harmful to the system," a private bank securities manager.

Bond portfolios of Turkish banks rose to 835.3 trillion lira at the end of 1996, up 223 percent from end-1995. Total deposits stood at 2,606 trillion lira at the end of 1996, up 133 percent from a year ago.
Turkey's domestic debt stood at 2,958 trillion lira at the end of November 1996, up 117.3 percent from end-1995.

The downward trend in t-bill and bond yields began in the last two days of 1996, after a government move to raise witholding tax on interest income from state securities to be issued in 1997 to 12 percent from previous 10 percent which was imposed on November 1, 1996.
A cabinet decision to delay the introduction of income tax on interest earnings from bonds and bills by one year to 1999 also boosted public and bank demand for outstanding state securities.

T-bill and bond yields have plunged more than 20 points to below 90 percent in the bond market since December 27, 1996, helped by expectations of lower inflation in 1997 and of success in reaching government budgetary and privatisation targets.
"The continuation of these optimistic expectations in the long term depends on the government's implementation and realisation of its budget and privatisation targets," Gurer said.
The sharp fall in bond market yields also diverted investors' attention to other alternatives, namely the dollar and the stock market, bankers said.
Following the dollar's strong gains in the world markets, the U.S. currency has risen by 7.1 percent against the Turkish lira since the beginning of this year.

Turkish shares surged 38.5 percent from January 2 to Thursday's all-time high close of 1,352, including Thursday's 8.07 percent jump caused by a constitutional court ruling which gave the green light for the sale of Turk Telekom, the centrepiece of the government's privatisation plans.
